title: Ex-Pharmacy Cashier Explains How Coupon Stacking Actually Works
creator: Jolene Park
description:
I worked a CVS register for four years. People always asked me why their coupons did or didn't go through, so here is everything I know about how the register actually decides.

I don't work there anymore and none of this is endorsed by anyone. Policies change and vary by state, ask at your store.

sentences.t: So for four years I stood behind a pharmacy register, and the number one question I got was, why didn't my coupon work?
And the honest answer was usually, the computer said no, and I couldn't do anything about it.
But I did learn how the computer thinks, so today I'm going to explain it, because it's actually kind of interesting.
There are basically three kinds of discounts that end up in your cart, and the register treats each one differently.
First, the store coupon, which is the one the store itself pays for.
Second, the manufacturer coupon, where the brand pays, and the store gets that money back later.
And third, store rewards, which at CVS are called ExtraBucks, and they basically work like store cash.
So let me read you a real example of what you'd see on one of those long receipts, and what each line actually means.
It says, twenty percent off your entire purchase, use code SPRING20 in the app or show this at the register.
That one's a store coupon, and it's applied to your total after almost everything else has already come off.
Then it'll say, spend thirty dollars on participating vitamins, get ten dollars ExtraBucks rewards.
That ten dollars doesn't come off today, it prints at the bottom, and you use it on your next trip, before it expires.
And then there's the classic, buy one get one fifty percent off, which the register counts as two items at a lower price each.
Okay, so here's the thing nobody tells you, the order matters.
If you hand me the percent off coupon first, and the ExtraBucks after, you can end up below the thirty dollars you needed.
And then the rewards don't print, and you get mad at me, and I get mad at the computer.
The register is supposed to sort it out, but in my experience it didn't always, so scan the rewards trigger first.
Stacking is where it gets fun, because a store coupon and a manufacturer coupon can usually go on the same item.
So if shampoo is on sale, and you have a store coupon, and a manufacturer coupon, you can get all three.
What you can't do is use two manufacturer coupons on one item, the register catches that every single time.
Now, the stuff that always failed, and I mean always.
Expired coupons, obviously, and no, I couldn't override them, my manager could, sometimes, if she liked you.
Photocopied coupons, the barcode would scan and then the register would flag it, and I'd have to give it back.
Coupons for a specific size, like the twelve ounce, when you grabbed the sixteen ounce, the computer is very literal.
And my personal favorite, people trying to use a coupon from a totally different store chain.
Bless them, but no.
So, my honest advice after four years of watching people do this.
Don't buy something just because there's a coupon for it, that's how the store wins.
Make your list first, then look for coupons for things already on the list.
And please be nice to your cashier, we didn't write the rules, we're just the ones who have to say no.
If you've got a coupon question I didn't answer, leave it in the comments and I'll do a part two.
